title: Davydenko, Kolbuszewska & Peetz (2021), 'A meta-analysis of financial self-control strategies', PLOS ONE 16(7):e0253938, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0253938 — VERIFIED 2026-09-05 by full fetch. Key facts: 29 studies / 12 self-control strategies; overall d = 0.57 (95% CI 0.43–0.71, Z = 8.38, p < .001); sensitivity check without largest study (n=8,940) d = 0.59; proactive d = 0.56 [0.30–0.83] vs reactive d = 0.58 [0.43–0.72], strategy type not a significant moderator (p = .930). Tracking-related studies in the evidence base include 'tracking weekly saving deposits' (Akbas et al. 2016) and 'tracking expenses via text messages' (Hernández Escuer et al. 2014).

Soman (2001), 'Effects of Payment Mechanism on Spending Behavior: The Role of Rehearsal and Immediacy of Payments', Journal of Consumer Research 27(4):460–474 — VERIFIED 2026-09-05 via search-result citation records (PsycNet 2001-00910-005; RePEc oup:jconrs v27 y2001 i4 p460-74). Key fact: payment mechanisms requiring greater REHEARSAL (e.g. writing down the amount paid) and greater immediacy make past payments more accessible in memory and reduce subsequent spending; less transparent mechanisms (credit card) lead to overspending. This is the peer-reviewed mechanism for why manually recording an expense increases its psychological weight.

Soman (2003), 'The Effect of Payment Transparency on Consumption: Quasi-Experiments from the Field', Marketing Letters 14(3):173–183, DOI 10.1023/A:1027444717586 — VERIFIED 2026-09-05 via search records (~459 citations). NOTE: this is Marketing Letters, NOT JCR (common misattribution). Key fact: the lower the payment 'transparency' (vividness of the act of payment), the greater subsequent consumption; effect weaker for third-party charges (hotel accounts) — the mechanism behind automated/decoupled charges such as recurring subscriptions.

Prelec & Loewenstein (1998), 'The Red and the Black: Mental Accounting of Savings and Debt', Marketing Science 17(1):4–28 — VERIFIED 2026-09-05 via citation records. Key fact: origin of 'pain of paying' and the coupling/decoupling model; decoupling payment from consumption (credit, prepaid, subscriptions) reduces the felt hedonic cost of purchases. Cited via Marketing Science 17:4–28 (widely misattributed to JCR).

Prelec & Simester (2001), 'Always Leave Home Without It: A Further Investigation of the Credit-Card Effect on Willingness to Pay', Marketing Letters 12(1):5–12 — VERIFIED 2026-09-05 via MIT Simester paper listing. Augenblick, Jack, Kaur, Masiye & Swanson (2026), 'Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing', NBER Working Paper 35430, DOI 10.3386/w35430 (AEA RCT registry AEARCTR-0004409) — VERIFIED 2026-09-05 by abstract fetch. Key facts: individuals underestimate upcoming spending by ~50%; a randomized 'think through future expenses associatively in categories' intervention (no new information) raised remembered expenses by 36–60%, lowered immediate spending, raised savings 15% six weeks later, and funded 9% higher next-year crop revenue; replicated among low-income Americans.

Sussman & Alter (2012), 'The Exception Is the Rule: Underestimating and Overspending on Exceptional Expenses', Journal of Consumer Research 39(4):800–814 — VERIFIED 2026-09-05 via Adam Alter's NYU Stern publication listing (OUP page 403s anonymous fetches). Key fact: consumers underestimate exceptional (irregular/discretionary) expenses relative to ordinary ones and consequently overspend when they occur. DIRECTION of underestimation: exceptional/discretionary spending is the systematically under-estimated part.

tauri-plugin-dialog v2 source, src/commands.rs — VERIFIED 2026-09-05 by raw fetch. KEY ANSWER: plugin-dialog AUTOMATICALLY grants fs scope at runtime after every pick: for directory selection it calls `s.allow_directory(&path, options.recursive)` on the window fs scope (and `tauri_scope.allow_directory`); for file open/save it calls `s.allow_file(&path)`. CRITICAL NUANCE: subdirectory (recursive) access only when the open options ALSO pass `recursive: true` — OpenDialogOptions.recursive: 'If directory is true, indicates that it will be read recursively later. Defines whether subdirectories will be allowed on the scope or not' — default false. So open({directory:true, recursive:true}) is required for a watch-recursive-capable grant; FsExt::allow_directory in Rust is only needed for scopes the user didn't pick.

Superuser 'FileSystemWatcher does not react to changes in excel file' + StackOverflow 43080981 + notify-rs/notify issues #129 (temp-file Create/Rename ordering on Windows) and #261 (coarse ModifyKind on Windows) — VERIFIED 2026-09-05 via search records. KEY ANSWER: Excel saves are NOT Modify(Data) events — Excel writes a temp file then renames it over the original (ReadDirectoryChangesW reports it as Rename; .NET FileSystemWatcher users see 'Renamed' events, and notify on Windows has the same backend). Practical rules for CapyExpense's Tauri watch: treat ANY event touching the watched path (EventKind::Modify(ModifyKind::Name(RenameMode::Both/To)), Create, Modify) as a save signal and re-read content; pass a delayMs debounce (e.g. 300–500ms) to collapse the event burst; ignore Excel's '~$' lock files and '.tmp' siblings; WSL caveat (notify #254) irrelevant inside Tauri on native Windows.

Lambrecht & Skiera (2006), 'Paying Too Much and Being Happy About It: Existence, Causes, and Consequences of Tariff-Choice Biases', Journal of Marketing Research 43(2):212–223 — VERIFIED 2026-09-05 via SAGE/PsycNet/SSRN records (~612 citations). Key fact: 'flat-rate bias' — consumers systematically pick flat-rate plans over cheaper metered ones (causes: insurance effect, taxi-meter effect, usage overestimation) and flat-rate-biased customers churn LESS — recurring flat charges are psychologically comfortable and avoid re-evaluation. Underwrites why small recurring charges escape scrutiny.
